short.headline: About 100 pedestrians a day were recorded as killed in 2024
short.dek: The annual report counts 36,526 pedestrian deaths. It maps the victims and collisions but cannot measure the danger of a walking journey.
short.body: Pedestrians were one in five people recorded as killed on India’s roads in 2024. The police count rose 3.7 per cent from 2023. Older victims were more often pedestrians within their age group’s road-death total, but no national data here count the walking trips needed for a per-journey risk rate.

macha.heading: Okay, macha, how risky is a walk?
macha.body: The police recorded 36,526 pedestrian deaths in 2024. That is about 100 people a day. The report tells us their ages, where the largest state totals were and what vehicles were recorded in their collisions. It cannot tell you the chance of dying on your next walk, because it never counts how much walking people did.
macha.soWhat: Treat the death count as a map for investigation. A walking-risk rate needs walking journeys or distance and better linked crash records.

article.title: How safe is it to walk on India’s roads?
article.standfirst: About 100 pedestrians a day were recorded as killed in 2024. MoRTH’s tables reveal who they were and what struck them. They still cannot tell us the risk of a walking journey.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## How many pedestrians are killed on India's roads?

MoRTH's police returns record **36,526 pedestrians killed in road crashes in 2024**. That is one in five of the 177,175 people recorded as killed on India's roads, and close to 100 pedestrian deaths a day in a leap year. Only two-wheeler users form a larger victim group in this national table.

A pedestrian is the person recorded as walking when they were killed. The label does not describe who caused the collision. It also does not tell us how dangerous a walk is compared with a ride or drive. To answer that, we would need deaths divided by the number or distance of walking journeys, alongside the same measure for other forms of travel. The report does not provide those denominators. The count still matters: it says that walking is involved in a large share of the road-death record, even before we know the chance of harm on any one trip. The [broader road-death article](/articles/who-dies-on-indias-roads/) places this toll beside the other road-user groups.

## Is the pedestrian toll falling?

No, at least in the latest comparison the report provides. Recorded pedestrian deaths rose from 35,221 in 2023 to 36,526 in 2024, an increase of 1,305 people or 3.7 per cent. Pedestrians made up 20.4 per cent of reported road deaths in 2023 and 20.6 per cent in 2024. The share moved little while the number of people lost rose.

Two years do not establish a persistent trend. Counts can move with travel volume, crash severity and reporting. A longer series would require joining annual reports carefully. MoRTH says it changed the format for identifying victim road users from 2019. Earlier reports had classified deaths primarily by the impacting vehicle. We should not splice pre-2019 labels into this series as though they meant the same thing. This article stays with the 2024 victim data and the report's direct 2023 comparison.

## How old were the pedestrians who died?

The largest published age band is 45–60, with 8,436 pedestrian deaths. Another 6,160 victims were 60 or older, and 1,888 were younger than 18. The age of 792 pedestrians was recorded as unknown. The chart leaves that group visible. These counts sum to all 36,526 recorded pedestrian deaths.

The distribution resists a simple story that walking deaths belong to only one stage of life. Children, working-age adults and older people all appear. The report's age bands are broad, so we cannot see what happened at a particular birthday or estimate the risk of a school walk. Nor can we infer that a 60-year-old faces more danger per kilometre walked simply because an age band has more recorded deaths. Groups differ in size and in how much they walk. The next comparison asks a different, narrower question: among people killed on roads at each age, how many were pedestrians?

## Are older road victims more often pedestrians?

Yes, as a share of **recorded road deaths within the same age band**. Of the 14,767 people aged 60 and over killed in road crashes in 2024, 6,160 were pedestrians. That is 41.7 per cent. Among victims aged 18–25, 4,333 of 34,154 were pedestrians, or 12.7 per cent. The bars show that walking takes a different place in the victim mix at different ages.

The calculation matters. For each age band we divided pedestrian deaths by *all* road deaths in that band, then multiplied by 100. The denominator changes from band to band. A larger percentage among older victims could reflect how people travel, what happens when they are struck, or both. It is **not** the probability that an older person dies while walking. That would require counts of older people walking, their journeys or distance, and comparable exposure for other ages. The report supplies none of those.

## Were the pedestrians killed mostly men?

The police record lists 29,055 male and 7,471 female pedestrian victims in 2024. Men therefore account for 79.5 per cent of the recorded pedestrian deaths. Those figures come from the age-and-sex annexure and also appear in the report's own narrative, giving us a useful cross-check on a scanned table.

The split tells us who appears in the death record. It cannot tell us whether walking is more dangerous for a man than for a woman. We do not know how many trips each group made, when and where they walked, or how often they crossed high-traffic roads. It would be especially misleading to turn 79.5 per cent into a claim about who behaves carefully. The victim's sex is not a crash-cause field. The next table changes perspective again, from the person who died to the vehicle police recorded in the collision.

## What vehicles were recorded in pedestrian deaths?

Two-wheelers were the largest named impacting-vehicle group, recorded in 10,378 pedestrian deaths. Cars, taxis, vans and light motor vehicles appear in 9,302; trucks and lorries in 5,165. The “Others” category holds 7,857 deaths, more than one in five pedestrian victims. It mixes vehicle and other classifications, so it is a substantial blind spot rather than a single kind of crash.

MoRTH calls the recorded counterpart a “crime vehicle” in its table. The term is administrative. A row saying a pedestrian was struck by a two-wheeler is not a legal verdict about the rider. The national table does not record the street layout, crossing, speed or sequence of actions. Nor do the bars rank how dangerous each vehicle is per kilometre driven. They help identify which encounters need closer local study. A useful investigation would connect the crash record to the actual place where people crossed and vehicles moved.

## Where are the largest pedestrian death totals?

Tamil Nadu reports 4,712 pedestrian deaths in 2024, followed by Bihar with 4,149, Maharashtra with 3,344 and West Bengal with 3,241. The ten states shown in the chart account for 27,354 deaths, 74.9 per cent of the national pedestrian total. The remaining 9,172 deaths are spread across other states and union territories. Each displayed value was checked against the original scanned annexure; a second annexure's age-and-sex rows reconcile with the state totals.

These are counts of recorded loss, useful for deciding where more detailed reporting and investigation are needed. They are not a league table of how safe it is to walk. States differ in population, how much people walk, road networks, traffic and completeness of police reporting. Even a per-resident rate would miss differences in walking exposure. To compare the danger of a walking journey across states, we would need a consistent record of walking trips and pedestrian deaths. The national report provides the second half of that calculation, imperfectly, and not the first.

## Is this only a national-highway problem?

No. MoRTH records 11,386 pedestrian deaths on national highways in 2024, 31.2 per cent of the country's pedestrian total. Subtracting that count from 36,526 leaves 25,140 on **all other roads combined**. That second bar includes state highways and other roads; the source table does not break the pedestrian remainder into those categories here.

The larger off-highway count matters because a highway-only response would miss most recorded pedestrian deaths. It does not prove that another road type is more dangerous for a person walking. Highways and local roads carry very different volumes of traffic and pedestrian movement. The report gives no common exposure measure to divide the deaths by. The split points towards a broad street-and-road question: people walking need protection in many settings, and the national total alone does not tell us which crossing or stretch should be fixed first.

## What would make a walk safer?

The national MoRTH tables used here do not identify a single cause of these deaths. They do not tell us whether a victim had a usable footpath, where the nearest safe crossing was, how fast a vehicle was moving, or whether the pedestrian died after reaching hospital. Reading the impacting-vehicle row as a verdict on behaviour would skip the place where the collision happened.

The World Health Organization (WHO) [pedestrian-safety manual](https://www.who.int/publications/b/65858) describes the evidence behind separating pedestrians from traffic, reducing conflict at intersections and managing speed through road design, enforcement and other measures. Those are general findings, not measurements of India's 2024 streets or proof that a named measure would have prevented every death in this report. For an Indian city or district, the next step is local: connect police deaths to road geometry, pedestrian movement, traffic speed and care after the crash. A national annual PDF can locate the burden. It cannot substitute for that street-level account.

## How should you read these figures?

The death counts come from MoRTH's *Road Accidents in India 2024*, assembled from state and union-territory police returns. Table 4.4 supplies the 2023–24 pedestrian totals and road-user comparison. Annexure 33 supplies pedestrian age and sex; Table 4.2 supplies all road deaths by age for the within-age percentages. Table 4.5 and Annexure 29(a) classify the vehicles recorded in pedestrian collisions and give state totals. Table 2.11 supplies pedestrian deaths on national highways. We used the original PDF, checked every plotted observation, and reconciled age, sex and state totals. The scanned annexures were read with a model only as a transcription aid; the displayed cells were checked against the original page images.

Shares of all 2024 road deaths divide by **177,175**. Pedestrian-only shares divide by **36,526**. The age-composition chart divides pedestrian deaths in each age band by all road deaths in that *same* band. “Other roads combined” is 36,526 minus 11,386 national-highway pedestrian deaths. None of these operations yields deaths per walking journey or per kilometre walked. The 2023–24 comparison is short by design because victim classification changed in 2019. WHO's manual provides general evidence on pedestrian protection, not an India-specific exposure denominator. Police reporting can miss deaths, especially if a later hospital death is not linked back to the crash record.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A person recorded as walking when involved in the road crash. It describes the victim’s road use, not who caused the collision.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The same death can also appear in a table by impacting vehicle.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: How many walking journeys people made, or how far they walked.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Without this, a death count cannot become a risk per trip.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The vehicle police recorded as the collision counterpart to a victim.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: This administrative label is not a court finding of fault.

chartExplainers.visualId: One in five recorded road deaths was a pedestrian
chartExplainers.title: One in five recorded road deaths was a pedestrian
chartExplainers.takeaway: Pedestrians account for 36,526 of 177,175 recorded deaths in 2024.
chartExplainers.detail: Only two-wheeler users have a larger count. Road-user groups identify the people killed; they do not identify the person responsible for a collision.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The reader needs to see the pedestrian toll within the full road-death record.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is a victim road-user group, all for India in 2024.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: A death share is not the chance of dying on a journey.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Long road-user names wrap; the count stays beside each bar.

chartExplainers.title: Pedestrian deaths rose again in 2024
chartExplainers.takeaway: The police count rose from 35,221 to 36,526 in one year.
chartExplainers.detail: That is 1,305 additional recorded deaths, or 3.7 per cent. The two years use the same victim-category definition in this report.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The direct comparison tests whether the toll was falling at the latest point.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the two calendar-year bars together; they are counts of people, not crashes.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Two annual counts cannot establish a long-run trend or per-trip risk.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Both years have a printed value alongside the bar.

chartExplainers.visualId: Deaths of pedestrians span every age group
chartExplainers.title: Deaths of pedestrians span every age group
chartExplainers.takeaway: The 45–60 band records 8,436 pedestrian deaths, and 6,160 victims were 60 or older.
chartExplainers.detail: The report also records 1,888 victims under 18 and 792 whose age was unknown. The published bands sum to all pedestrian victims.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Age gives the toll a human distribution before any attempt at comparison.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read each published age band as a count of pedestrians killed; unknown age remains separate.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: A count by age does not measure the risk of a walk for that age.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep the Age unknown row visible when comparing the other bars.

chartExplainers.visualId: Walking victims make up a larger share of road deaths at older ages
chartExplainers.title: Walking victims make up a larger share of road deaths at older ages
chartExplainers.takeaway: Pedestrians were 41.7 per cent of road victims aged 60 and over, compared with 12.7 per cent at 18–25.
chartExplainers.detail: Each bar divides pedestrian deaths by all road deaths in the same published age band. The denominator changes with age; no walking exposure is measured.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This same-age comparison asks a different question from the raw age counts.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Values are percentages of road deaths within each age band, not percentages of all pedestrians.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The chart does not give the chance of dying while walking.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Read the unit in the heading: per cent of road deaths in that age band.

chartExplainers.visualId: Four in five recorded pedestrian victims were men
chartExplainers.title: Four in five recorded pedestrian victims were men
chartExplainers.takeaway: Police recorded 29,055 male and 7,471 female pedestrian deaths in 2024.
chartExplainers.detail: The two groups sum to the national pedestrian total and match the report narrative. Sex is a description of victims, not a measure of how often each group walked.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The sex split adds another dimension to the people behind the total.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Both bars count people killed in the report’s male and female categories.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not infer comparative walking risk or carefulness without travel exposure.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Both bars use a zero baseline and have direct values.

chartExplainers.visualId: Two-wheelers and cars figure prominently in pedestrian deaths
chartExplainers.title: Two-wheelers and cars figure prominently in pedestrian deaths
chartExplainers.takeaway: Two-wheelers appear in 10,378 pedestrian deaths and cars, taxis, vans and LMVs in 9,302.
chartExplainers.detail: The mixed Others group contains 7,857 deaths, so a large part of the police classification remains vague. Impacting vehicle is a police field, not a legal finding of fault.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The other vehicle involved is a different question from the victim’s road-user type.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Eight impacting-vehicle categories partition the 36,526 pedestrian victims.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The bars cannot rank vehicles by danger per kilometre driven or assign blame.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The long car and Others labels wrap; their counts remain visible.

chartExplainers.visualId: Ten states account for three-quarters of pedestrian deaths
chartExplainers.title: Ten states account for three-quarters of pedestrian deaths
chartExplainers.takeaway: The ten displayed state totals add to 27,354 pedestrian deaths, or 74.9 per cent nationally.
chartExplainers.detail: Tamil Nadu records 4,712 and Bihar 4,149. The chart selects the ten largest counts from Annexure 29(a); other states and union territories are omitted.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The state lens shows where a large local evidence task would sit.
chartExplainers.howToRead: These are selected raw totals, not rates; they do not partition the entire national toll.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Without walking journeys or distance, a state ranking is not a safety ranking.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Long state names wrap and every bar keeps its value.

chartExplainers.visualId: Most pedestrian deaths were recorded off national highways
chartExplainers.title: Most pedestrian deaths were recorded off national highways
chartExplainers.takeaway: National highways account for 11,386 pedestrian deaths, leaving 25,140 on all other roads combined.
chartExplainers.detail: The remainder is the national pedestrian total minus the national-highway pedestrian row. It mixes state highways and other road classes because this source does not split the pedestrian remainder here.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The road-class split prevents a highway-only reading of the pedestrian toll.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The two bars partition the 2024 pedestrian deaths into national highways and every other road.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: No road category has a matched walking-exposure denominator.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The second label means all non-national-highway roads combined.
